http-status-codes.desc-continue: The client should continue with the rest of the request
http-status-codes.desc-switchingProtocols: The server agrees to switch to the requested protocol
http-status-codes.desc-processing: The request was received and is still being processed (WebDAV)
http-status-codes.desc-earlyHints: Preliminary response headers sent for preloading
http-status-codes.desc-ok: The request succeeded and the response contains the result
http-status-codes.desc-created: The request succeeded and a new resource was created
http-status-codes.desc-accepted: The request was accepted but has not been processed yet
http-status-codes.desc-nonAuthoritative: The response comes from a cache or third party, not the origin server
http-status-codes.desc-noContent: The request succeeded with an empty response body
http-status-codes.desc-resetContent: The request succeeded; ask the client to reset the document view
http-status-codes.desc-partialContent: A Range request returned part of the resource
http-status-codes.desc-multipleChoices: The requested resource has multiple possible locations
http-status-codes.desc-movedPermanently: The resource has permanently moved to a new URL
http-status-codes.desc-found: The resource temporarily lives at a different URL
http-status-codes.desc-seeOther: Fetch the resource from another URL using GET
http-status-codes.desc-notModified: The resource is unchanged; use the client's cached copy
http-status-codes.desc-temporaryRedirect: The resource temporarily lives elsewhere; keep method and body
http-status-codes.desc-permanentRedirect: The resource has permanently moved; keep method and body
http-status-codes.desc-badRequest: The request is malformed and cannot be understood
http-status-codes.desc-paymentRequired: Reserved; usually means payment is needed
http-status-codes.desc-forbidden: The server refuses to fulfill the request
http-status-codes.desc-notFound: The server cannot find the requested resource
http-status-codes.desc-methodNotAllowed: The request method is not supported by the resource
http-status-codes.desc-notAcceptable: No response matches the Accept headers
http-status-codes.desc-proxyAuthenticationRequired: Authenticate with the proxy server first
http-status-codes.desc-requestTimeout: The server timed out waiting for the request
http-status-codes.desc-conflict: The request conflicts with the current state of the resource
http-status-codes.desc-gone: The resource has been permanently removed
http-status-codes.desc-lengthRequired: The Content-Length request header is missing
http-status-codes.desc-preconditionFailed: A request precondition in the headers was not met
http-status-codes.desc-payloadTooLarge: The request body exceeds the size the server allows
http-status-codes.desc-uriTooLong: The request URI is longer than the server can process
http-status-codes.desc-unsupportedMediaType: The request Content-Type is not supported
http-status-codes.desc-rangeNotSatisfiable: The requested Range exceeds the size of the resource
http-status-codes.desc-expectationFailed: The requirement of the Expect header cannot be met
http-status-codes.desc-imATeapot: April Fools joke; the server refuses to brew coffee
http-status-codes.desc-misdirectedRequest: The request was sent to a server unable to produce a response
http-status-codes.desc-upgradeRequired: The client must switch to a higher protocol version
http-status-codes.desc-preconditionRequired: The request must include conditional headers
http-status-codes.desc-tooManyRequests: Rate limit triggered; the client sent too many requests
http-status-codes.desc-requestHeaderFieldsTooLarge: The request headers exceed the server's limits
http-status-codes.desc-unavailableForLegalReasons: Access to the resource was denied for legal reasons
http-status-codes.desc-internalServerError: The server hit an unexpected error
http-status-codes.desc-notImplemented: The server does not support the functionality required
http-status-codes.desc-badGateway: The upstream server returned an invalid response
http-status-codes.desc-serviceUnavailable: The server is overloaded or under maintenance
http-status-codes.desc-gatewayTimeout: The upstream server did not respond in time
http-status-codes.desc-httpVersionNotSupported: The HTTP version used by the request is not supported
http-status-codes.desc-insufficientStorage: The server ran out of storage to complete the request (WebDAV)
http-status-codes.desc-networkAuthenticationRequired: The client must authenticate to gain network access

sql-memo.title: SQL Cheat Sheet
sql-memo.description: MySQL 8 syntax, functions, indexes, transactions and cross-dialect differences, with MySQL and PostgreSQL install guides
sql-memo.layers-desc: Split by purpose: define, manipulate, query, control access, control transactions
sql-memo.write-order-desc: How a standard SELECT is written
sql-memo.exec-order-desc: The order the engine actually evaluates, which decides where aliases work
sql-memo.exec-order-note: SELECT is produced after WHERE, so a column alias cannot be used in WHERE, but usually works in GROUP BY and ORDER BY
sql-memo.comments-desc: Three comment forms plus optimizer hints
sql-memo.identifiers-desc: Wrap names that collide with reserved words in backticks
sql-memo.identifiers-note: lower_case_table_names decides case sensitivity for database and table names and must be set before initializing the data directory; changing it later breaks startup
sql-memo.identifiers-diff: PostgreSQL and Oracle use double quotes, SQL Server uses brackets; unquoted identifiers fold to lowercase in PostgreSQL and uppercase in Oracle
sql-memo.null-logic-desc: NULL means unknown, so any comparison with it yields UNKNOWN, not true or false
sql-memo.null-logic-note: A single NULL inside a NOT IN subquery makes the whole condition never match; COUNT(col) skips NULL while COUNT(*) does not
sql-memo.sel-columns-desc: Fetch only what you need; the precondition for covering indexes
sql-memo.sel-star-note: Avoid in production: extra IO, no covering index, and a schema change silently breaks the row mapping
sql-memo.sel-expr-desc: Compute in the select list and name the result with AS
sql-memo.sel-expr-note: Indexing an expression needs a function index (8.0.13+) or a generated column
sql-memo.sel-table-alias-desc: AS is optional; required for self joins
sql-memo.sel-distinct-desc: Deduplicate whole result rows at the cost of sorting or hashing
sql-memo.sel-distinct-multi-desc: DISTINCT applies to every column that follows it
sql-memo.sel-where-desc: Row-level filter; prefer half-open intervals for time ranges
sql-memo.sel-order-note: Without a unique sort key, paging drops or repeats rows; always append a tiebreaker column
sql-memo.sel-limit-desc: Cap the row count and set an offset
sql-memo.sel-limit-diff: PostgreSQL also uses LIMIT/OFFSET; SQL Server and Oracle 12c+ use OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY and require ORDER BY; SQL Server can also use TOP (n)
sql-memo.op-arithmetic-desc: Add, subtract, multiply, divide and modulo; DIV is integer division
sql-memo.op-comparison-desc: Standard <> and non-standard != are synonyms; <=> is MySQL's null-safe equality
sql-memo.op-comparison-note: Any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN; only <=> can test NULL equality, and comparing numbers with strings triggers a cast that kills the index
sql-memo.op-logical-note: Precedence is NOT > AND > OR, so add parentheses when mixing; OR across unindexed columns degrades to a full scan
sql-memo.op-between-note: BETWEEN on the last day of a range loses rows with a time component; use >= start AND < day-after-end
sql-memo.op-in-desc: Set membership with a literal list or a subquery
sql-memo.op-in-note: Values must match the column type or the implicit cast disables the index; NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery yields NULL — use NOT EXISTS
sql-memo.op-like-desc: % matches any run of characters, _ matches exactly one
sql-memo.op-like-note: A leading wildcard cannot use an index; escape a literal % with ESCAPE
sql-memo.op-like-diff: SQL Server's LIKE supports [abc] ranges, PostgreSQL has ILIKE for case-insensitive matching, Oracle's LIKE is case-sensitive
sql-memo.op-null-test-desc: IS NULL / IS NOT NULL / IS TRUE / IS FALSE / IS UNKNOWN
sql-memo.op-quantifier-desc: Compare against a subquery result set
sql-memo.op-quantifier-note: Semantics shift when the subquery contains NULL; a scalar aggregate such as MAX() is easier to reason about
sql-memo.op-bitwise-desc: AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts
sql-memo.op-bitwise-diff: SQL Server has no ^ for bitwise XOR and Oracle has no ^ at all (use BITAND)
sql-memo.join-inner-desc: Keeps only rows matching on both sides
sql-memo.join-left-desc: Keeps all left rows, filling NULL when the right side misses
sql-memo.join-left-note: Filtering the nullable side in WHERE silently turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN; put the condition in ON
sql-memo.join-full-desc: Keeps unmatched rows from both sides
sql-memo.join-full-note: MySQL and SQL Server have no FULL OUTER JOIN; emulate it with LEFT UNION RIGHT and make sure both sides expose identical columns
sql-memo.join-full-diff: PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite support FULL [OUTER] JOIN natively
sql-memo.join-natural-desc: Auto-joins on every identically named column
sql-memo.join-natural-note: Adding a same-named column changes the result silently; never use it in production
sql-memo.join-self-desc: Join a table to itself for parent-child relations
sql-memo.join-using-desc: USING is shorthand when both sides share the column name
sql-memo.join-using-note: The shared column appears only once in the result, so SELECT * differs from the ON form
sql-memo.join-multi-desc: Chained JOINs; watch which table the optimizer picks first
sql-memo.join-anti-desc: Find left rows with no match on the right
sql-memo.join-anti-note: LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and NOT EXISTS both beat NOT IN on a subquery
sql-memo.join-semi-desc: Return left rows that have at least one match, without duplication
sql-memo.join-semi-note: Expressed with IN or EXISTS; cheaper than JOIN followed by DISTINCT
sql-memo.join-lateral-desc: The right side may reference columns of the current left row
sql-memo.join-lateral-note: MySQL supports LATERAL from 8.0.14; older versions need a correlated subquery
sql-memo.join-lateral-diff: SQL Server expresses the same idea with CROSS APPLY / OUTER APPLY
sql-memo.gb-basic-desc: Group rows by value, then aggregate
sql-memo.gb-multi-desc: Group by the combination of columns
sql-memo.gb-having-desc: Filter rows before grouping with WHERE, groups after with HAVING
sql-memo.gb-having-note: Keep filters in WHERE whenever possible; HAVING runs after aggregation and thus scans more
sql-memo.gb-alias-desc: MySQL lets GROUP BY reference a select-list alias or column number
sql-memo.gb-alias-diff: PostgreSQL accepts the alias but not the position; SQL Server and Oracle require the raw column or expression
sql-memo.gb-rollup-note: Rolled-up dimensions show as NULL; use GROUPING() to tell them apart from real NULLs, and note that ROLLUP cannot be combined with ORDER BY
sql-memo.gb-rollup-diff: PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle use the function form ROLLUP(a,b) rather than the WITH ROLLUP keyword, and also offer CUBE and GROUPING SETS
sql-memo.gb-only-full-desc: Every non-aggregated select column must appear in GROUP BY
sql-memo.gb-only-full-note: On by default since 8.0; add the column to GROUP BY, wrap it in an aggregate or use ANY_VALUE() instead of disabling the mode
sql-memo.gb-any-value-desc: Tell the optimizer you accept an arbitrary value from the group
sql-memo.gb-any-value-note: MySQL-only and non-deterministic within a group; hurts portability
sql-memo.agg-count-note: COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) are identical; COUNT(col) skips NULL, so picking the smallest secondary index is the fastest count
sql-memo.agg-sum-desc: Adds values, ignoring NULL; returns NULL when everything is NULL
sql-memo.agg-sum-note: Wrap it in IFNULL(SUM(x), 0) so an empty set does not poison the whole expression
sql-memo.agg-avg-note: AVG ignores NULL instead of counting it as zero; to average over all rows use SUM(IF(cond, x, 0)) / COUNT(*)
sql-memo.agg-minmax-desc: Extremes; with GROUP BY they pick the newest key per group
sql-memo.agg-group-concat-desc: Join group values into one string with separator, ordering and DISTINCT
sql-memo.agg-group-concat-note: Output length is capped by group_concat_max_len (1024 by default) and is truncated with a warning
sql-memo.agg-group-concat-diff: PostgreSQL and SQL Server 2017+ use STRING_AGG, Oracle uses LISTAGG
sql-memo.agg-json-desc: Collect group rows into a JSON array or object
sql-memo.agg-json-note: Available since 8.0; element order is not guaranteed, so sort in a derived table first when order matters
sql-memo.agg-filter-desc: Attach a row filter to an aggregate
sql-memo.agg-filter-diff: MySQL has no FILTER clause; write SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) instead. PostgreSQL and SQLite support FILTER
sql-memo.agg-avg-desc: Average value, NULL rows are skipped
sql-memo.c-fk-actions-note: In MySQL NO ACTION behaves exactly like RESTRICT (no deferred checking); cascade actions do not fire row triggers
sql-memo.dt-parts-note: DAYOFWEEK numbers Sunday as 1 while WEEKDAY numbers Monday as 0 — the two are easy to mix up
sql-memo.idx-show-note: CARDINALITY is a sample estimate; run ANALYZE TABLE after big data swings to make it trustworthy
sql-memo.p-analyze-note: For InnoDB, OPTIMIZE TABLE is really a table rebuild; size the cost before running it on a large table
sql-memo.pg-maintain-note: PostgreSQL keeps dead row versions for MVCC, so write-heavy tables need timely VACUUM or they bloat
sql-memo.pr-design-note: Soft deletes complicate every unique constraint (you must include deleted_at) and keep growing the index; archive to a history table at scale
sql-memo.r-vars-note: Session variables with @ survive across statements, @@ are system variables, and DECLARE locals live only inside the current BEGIN block
sql-memo.str-case-pad-note: LPAD truncates instead of erroring when the string is already longer than the target width
sql-memo.str-format-note: FORMAT depends on locale and is slow, so avoid it for exports; TO_BASE64 inserts line breaks every 76 characters
sql-memo.str-length-note: One CJK character takes three bytes in utf8mb4: use CHAR_LENGTH for limits and LENGTH for byte checks
sql-memo.str-replace-note: Whether REPLACE is case-sensitive depends on the column collation; _bin is strict
sql-memo.str-sub-desc: Positions start at 1; a start of 0 or a negative count takes from the right
sql-memo.str-sub-diff: Oracle's SUBSTR matches MySQL; SQL Server's SUBSTRING rejects negative starts; PostgreSQL adds split_part
sql-memo.str-pos-desc: Returns the 1-based position or 0 when absent
sql-memo.str-trim-desc: Strip spaces or a given substring from either end
sql-memo.str-case-pad-desc: Upper, lower, left and right padding
sql-memo.str-format-desc: Thousands separators, hex, base64 and code points
sql-memo.str-regex-desc: Match, extract, replace and locate with regular expressions
sql-memo.str-regex-note: 8.0 switched from PCRE to ICU, so a few escapes behave differently than in 5.7; case sensitivity follows the collation
sql-memo.str-regex-diff: PostgreSQL uses ~ / ~* and regexp_replace, Oracle uses the REGEXP_LIKE family, SQL Server needs CLR
sql-memo.str-collate-sort-note: Applying COLLATE to a column disables index usage for it; switch the column to a _bin collation if you always need exact matching
sql-memo.str-split-rows-title: Split a delimited string into rows
sql-memo.str-split-rows-desc: MySQL has no SPLIT(); use JSON_TABLE instead
sql-memo.str-split-rows-note: Wrap the value into a valid JSON array first; PostgreSQL offers string_to_array and unnest
sql-memo.win-over-desc: Aggregation stops collapsing rows and decorates each row instead
sql-memo.win-over-note: Window functions are only allowed in SELECT and ORDER BY, never in WHERE; filter them from an outer query
sql-memo.win-running-desc: With ORDER BY the frame accumulates from the start of the partition to the current row
sql-memo.win-running-note: The default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW and includes peers, so tied rows share the same result
sql-memo.win-frame-desc: Pin down exactly which rows feed the aggregate
sql-memo.win-frame-note: MySQL 8.0 supports only ROWS and RANGE: physical offsets use ROWS, value intervals use RANGE
sql-memo.win-frame-diff: GROUPS and the EXCLUDE clause belong to PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server 2022+; MySQL rejects them
sql-memo.win-topn-desc: Number the rows, then filter in an outer query
sql-memo.win-topn-note: You cannot put a window function in WHERE, so wrap it in a derived table or CTE first
sql-memo.win-dedupe-desc: Keep the largest id per key and drop the rest
sql-memo.win-dedupe-note: Expensive on big tables: select the primary keys first, then delete in batches
sql-memo.win-ntile-desc: Split a partition into N buckets and compute cumulative distribution
sql-memo.win-lag-lead-desc: Read the previous or following row for period comparisons
sql-memo.win-lag-lead-note: Missing rows yield NULL and the third argument supplies a default; guard divisions with NULLIF
sql-memo.win-lag-lead-diff: MySQL only accepts RESPECT NULLS and errors on IGNORE NULLS; SQL Server 2022+ and Oracle support IGNORE NULLS; PostgreSQL implements neither
sql-memo.win-first-last-desc: Value of the first, last or Nth row of the frame
sql-memo.win-first-last-note: With ORDER BY, the default frame ends at the current row, so LAST_VALUE looks like the row itself; spell out ROWS UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING to truly reach the end
sql-memo.win-named-desc: Define a window once and reuse it
sql-memo.win-named-note: A named window may only be referenced by definitions that follow it
sql-memo.sq-scalar-desc: One row, one column, usable in SELECT, WHERE or SET
sql-memo.sq-scalar-note: More than one row raises error 1242; it runs once per outer row, so rewrite to a join at scale
sql-memo.sq-derived-desc: A subquery acting as a temporary table
sql-memo.sq-derived-note: A derived table must have an alias (error 1248 otherwise); 8.0 tries to merge it into the outer query via derived_merge
sql-memo.sq-in-desc: Match against a set produced by a query
sql-memo.sq-in-note: The optimizer usually applies a semi-join transformation; NOT IN returns nothing when the subquery yields NULL, so prefer NOT EXISTS
sql-memo.sq-exists-desc: Only cares whether a match exists, ignoring projected columns
sql-memo.sq-exists-note: Stops scanning at the first match, typically cheaper than JOIN plus DISTINCT
sql-memo.sq-correlated-desc: The inner query references outer columns and runs per row
sql-memo.sq-rewrite-desc: Safer and faster equivalents for NOT IN and scalar aggregates
sql-memo.sq-rewrite-note: Replace a per-row aggregate with a pre-aggregated derived table joined once
sql-memo.sq-row-desc: Match several columns at once with (a,b) IN ((1,2),(3,4))
sql-memo.sq-row-note: Range optimization on row constructors is limited; prefer a join on large sets
sql-memo.cte-basic-desc: Name a subquery for the current statement only
sql-memo.cte-basic-note: CTEs are not materialized and may be evaluated more than once; use a temp table for expensive results
sql-memo.cte-multi-desc: Comma-separated; later CTEs may reference earlier ones
sql-memo.cte-recursive-desc: Seed query UNION ALL recursive step, for series and hierarchies
sql-memo.cte-recursive-note: Column types come from the seed, so CAST long strings; depth is capped by cte_max_recursion_depth (1000 by default)
sql-memo.cte-tree-desc: Traverse from the root and accumulate depth and path
sql-memo.cte-tree-note: A parent cycle means infinite recursion; cap the level or track visited nodes
sql-memo.union-desc: Stack two selects vertically; column counts and types must align
sql-memo.union-all-desc: Concatenates without dedupe and is far faster
sql-memo.set-ops-desc: Intersection and difference; same precedence, evaluated left to right
sql-memo.set-ops-note: Non-comparable types such as BLOB or JSON cannot participate; the only ORDER BY belongs after the last query
sql-memo.set-ops-diff: INTERSECT / EXCEPT need MySQL 8.0.31+; other engines support them and Oracle spells the difference MINUS
sql-memo.num-round-desc: ROUND takes a scale, TRUNCATE cuts without carrying
sql-memo.num-round-note: MySQL rounds exact numerics away from zero; the approximate path defers to the C library, so results can differ from PostgreSQL
sql-memo.num-basic-desc: Absolute value, sign, modulo, pi and powers or logs
sql-memo.num-rand-desc: Random numbers, integers and global identifiers
sql-memo.num-rand-note: ORDER BY RAND() forces a full filesort; a UUID primary key fragments the clustered index — prefer ordered ids
sql-memo.num-greatest-desc: Max or min across the argument list
sql-memo.num-greatest-note: Any NULL argument makes the result NULL, the opposite of the NULL-skipping MIN/MAX aggregates
sql-memo.cast-desc: Explicit CAST / CONVERT and the implicit-cast trap
sql-memo.cast-note: In non-strict mode '12abc' silently becomes 12; casting an indexed column defeats the index
sql-memo.cast-diff: PostgreSQL prefers x::int; SQL Server's CONVERT takes the type first plus a style code; Oracle uses TO_CHAR / TO_NUMBER / TO_DATE
sql-memo.decimal-div-desc: Division yields DECIMAL with a scale driven by div_precision_increment
sql-memo.decimal-div-note: Integer division still produces a fraction — use DIV to truncate; keep money in DECIMAL to avoid float error
sql-memo.dt-now-desc: Statement time versus real system time
sql-memo.dt-now-note: NOW() is constant within a statement while SYSDATE() re-reads the clock; mixing them breaks replication
sql-memo.dt-parts-desc: Year through microsecond plus weekday and day-of-year
sql-memo.dt-add-desc: Nine base units plus eleven compound units
sql-memo.dt-add-diff: PostgreSQL writes now() + INTERVAL '1 month', SQL Server uses DATEADD(unit, n, d), Oracle uses ADD_MONTHS and plain addition
sql-memo.dt-diff-desc: DATEDIFF counts days, TIMESTAMPDIFF takes a unit
sql-memo.dt-diff-note: DATEDIFF(d1,d2) and TIMESTAMPDIFF(u,t1,t2) run in opposite directions, so reversed arguments produce negatives
sql-memo.dt-format-desc: Formatting and parsing share the same symbols
sql-memo.dt-format-note: %i is minutes and %f microseconds; STR_TO_DATE returns NULL on a mismatch instead of failing
sql-memo.dt-format-diff: PostgreSQL and Oracle use to_char templates (YYYY / MM / DD / HH24 / MI / SS); SQL Server uses FORMAT or CONVERT styles — none of the symbol sets are portable
sql-memo.dt-parse-desc: STR_TO_DATE by pattern, MAKEDATE and MAKETIME by components
sql-memo.dt-unix-desc: Convert between epoch seconds and DATETIME
sql-memo.dt-unix-note: UNIX_TIMESTAMP returns whole seconds; use NOW(3) for milliseconds, and FROM_UNIXTIME follows the session time zone
sql-memo.dt-tz-note: Named zones in CONVERT_TZ need the timezone tables loaded via mysql_tzinfo_to_sql, otherwise it returns NULL; storing UTC is the safe default
sql-memo.dt-range-desc: Only a half-open interval can use the index
sql-memo.dt-range-note: Wrapping the column in DATE() disables the index; compare the column itself against boundaries
sql-memo.dt-types-desc: Ranges and storage of the five types
sql-memo.dt-types-note: TIMESTAMP overflows in 2038 and its displayed value depends on the session time zone; prefer DATETIME(3) or store UTC
sql-memo.dt-default-desc: Fill on insert and refresh on update
sql-memo.dt-default-note: Keep only one ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP column, otherwise every update refreshes it
sql-memo.cond-case-when-desc: Multi-branch mapping and the most portable form
sql-memo.cond-case-when-note: CASE needs END; the first matching branch wins and the result type is merged across branches, so CAST each branch when it matters
sql-memo.cond-if-note: NULLIF(a,b) returns NULL when equal, the standard way to avoid division by zero; COALESCE takes any number of arguments
sql-memo.cond-if-diff: IF() and IFNULL() are MySQL; Oracle has NVL / NVL2 / DECODE, SQL Server has ISNULL / IIF — only COALESCE and CASE work everywhere
sql-memo.cond-bool-desc: A true condition is 1, so SUM gives a conditional count
sql-memo.cond-bool-note: MySQL has no real boolean type; other engines need a CASE rewrite
sql-memo.cond-is-null-func-diff: In SQL Server ISNULL(a,b) is a null-substitution function with completely different semantics; Oracle uses NVL; only IS NULL is portable
sql-memo.cond-branch-order-desc: With overlapping ranges, the first branch wins
sql-memo.json-extract-desc: -> yields JSON, ->> yields an unquoted scalar
sql-memo.json-extract-note: ->> is what you want for comparisons and indexes; a missing path returns NULL rather than failing
sql-memo.json-modify-desc: SET upserts, INSERT only adds, REPLACE only changes
sql-memo.json-query-desc: Containment, path existence, length, type and validation
sql-memo.json-table-desc: Map a JSON array into rows and columns
sql-memo.json-table-note: Needs 8.0.4+; declare a type per column and choose ERROR ON ERROR or DEFAULT for out-of-range values
sql-memo.json-table-diff: PostgreSQL uses jsonb_array_elements / json_to_recordset, SQL Server uses OPENJSON ... WITH
sql-memo.json-search-desc: Locate a value's path, with wildcards and array subscripts
sql-memo.json-index-note: A JSON column cannot be indexed directly; index a generated extraction instead, or a CAST(... AS ... ARRAY) multi-valued index for arrays
sql-memo.type-int-desc: Storage size and range of the five integers
sql-memo.type-int-note: The number in parentheses is display width, not a limit, and is deprecated since 8.0.17; choose BIGINT when unsure
sql-memo.type-decimal-note: FLOAT/DOUBLE are approximations (0.1 + 0.2 <> 0.3); store money as DECIMAL or as an integer in minor units
sql-memo.type-char-note: CHAR pads and loses trailing spaces, VARCHAR keeps them; TEXT cannot be defaulted and must be indexed with a prefix length
sql-memo.type-enum-desc: Pick one of a fixed list, stored as an ordinal
sql-memo.type-enum-note: An unknown value errors in strict mode and becomes '' otherwise; reordering members changes stored ordinals, so prefer a lookup table
sql-memo.type-json-desc: Binary storage with validation and field access
sql-memo.type-generated-desc: Virtual or stored columns derived from an expression
sql-memo.type-generated-note: VIRTUAL costs no row space but is computed on read; STORED takes space and can back a foreign key; both support secondary indexes
sql-memo.type-auto-desc: Auto counter and resetting the start value
sql-memo.type-auto-note: The counter only moves up and rollbacks leave gaps; since 8.0 the value survives a restart
sql-memo.type-auto-diff: PostgreSQL uses GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY or serial, SQL Server uses IDENTITY(1,1), Oracle 12c+ uses GENERATED AS IDENTITY or a SEQUENCE
sql-memo.cs-choose-title: Create a database with a charset
sql-memo.cs-choose-desc: Standardize on utf8mb4 with a 0900 collation
sql-memo.cs-choose-note: MySQL's utf8 is really utf8mb3 and cannot store emoji — always spell out utf8mb4
sql-memo.cs-levels-desc: Server, database, table, column and connection, each inheriting from the one above
sql-memo.cs-collation-desc: ci ignores case, bin compares bytes
sql-memo.cs-collation-note: Comparing or joining columns with different collations raises Illegal mix of collations and cannot use indexes
sql-memo.cs-convert-note: CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET rebuilds the table and can fail on row-size limits; estimate byte widths and run off-peak
sql-memo.cs-emoji-check-desc: Use HEX to confirm multibyte storage
sql-memo.cs-emoji-check-note: Proper bytes such as E4B8AD mean the chain is right; a 3F question mark means the connection layer already dropped the character
sql-memo.cs-where-desc: Add COLLATE to an expression for exact comparison
sql-memo.ins-basic-note: Omitting the column list binds you to physical order; adding a column breaks old statements, so always name columns
sql-memo.ins-set-note: Single row only, and it cannot be combined with a multi-value ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
sql-memo.ins-select-desc: Write a query result into another table
sql-memo.ins-ignore-desc: Downgrades errors to warnings and keeps going
sql-memo.ins-ignore-note: It also swallows truncation and foreign-key failures, so data disappears silently; do not treat it as an upsert
sql-memo.ins-upsert-desc: Update instead of failing on a key clash
sql-memo.ins-upsert-note: Triggers on any primary or unique key clash; affected rows are 1 for insert, 2 for update, 0 when the value is unchanged. VALUES() is deprecated since 8.0.20
sql-memo.ins-upsert-diff: PostgreSQL uses ON CONFLICT (col) DO UPDATE SET x = EXCLUDED.x; SQL Server and Oracle use MERGE, which MySQL lacks
sql-memo.ins-replace-note: It is a real DELETE + INSERT: the auto-increment id changes, triggers fire twice and unlisted columns reset to defaults
sql-memo.ins-lastid-title: Get the new id and row count
sql-memo.upd-basic-desc: Single-table update with optional ORDER BY and LIMIT batching
sql-memo.upd-basic-note: No WHERE means the whole table; with SQL_SAFE_UPDATES such statements are refused, and affected_rows only counts rows that actually changed
sql-memo.upd-join-note: Multi-table updates reject ORDER BY and LIMIT, and ambiguous column names may update the wrong table
sql-memo.del-basic-note: You cannot select from and delete the same table directly; wrap the subquery or use a join. Batch large deletes with LIMIT to bound undo and replication lag
sql-memo.truncate-desc: Compare their nature and side effects
sql-memo.truncate-note: TRUNCATE is DDL: it commits implicitly, cannot roll back and skips row triggers; a table referenced by a foreign key cannot be truncated
sql-memo.load-data-note: Needs the FILE privilege and is bound by secure_file_priv; LOCAL reads a client file and may be disabled server-side
sql-memo.ddl-create-desc: Columns, constraints, indexes and table options
sql-memo.ddl-engine-desc: Engine, charset, row format and comment
sql-memo.ddl-engine-note: InnoDB is the default; the row format caps index key length, so long utf8mb4 indexes need DYNAMIC
sql-memo.ddl-like-desc: LIKE copies indexes but no data
sql-memo.ddl-as-select-desc: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT copies data and column types only
sql-memo.ddl-as-select-note: Primary keys, indexes, defaults and auto-increment are not copied; add them afterwards
sql-memo.ddl-add-col-desc: Choose the position and add several at once
sql-memo.ddl-add-col-note: MySQL has no ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS (that is a MariaDB extension), so rerunning a script fails
sql-memo.ddl-modify-change-title: Change type or rename a column
sql-memo.ddl-modify-change-desc: MODIFY keeps the name, CHANGE renames
sql-memo.ddl-modify-change-note: CHANGE requires the full definition; forgetting NOT NULL, DEFAULT or COMMENT loses those attributes
sql-memo.ddl-drop-col-desc: Removes the column and its index prefixes
sql-memo.ddl-drop-col-diff: Oracle can defer the cost with SET UNUSED then DROP UNUSED COLUMNS; MySQL has no equivalent
sql-memo.ddl-comment-desc: Stored in metadata and read by tooling and code generators
sql-memo.ddl-rename-desc: RENAME TABLE can swap several tables in one statement
sql-memo.ddl-rename-note: Atomic rename is the finishing move of an online schema change: load a shadow table, then switch in an instant
sql-memo.ddl-online-desc: INSTANT, INPLACE and COPY, in rising cost
sql-memo.ddl-online-note: ALGORITHM is an assertion: MySQL errors out instead of silently downgrading; COPY blocks writes and INSTANT covers only a few operations
sql-memo.ddl-partition-desc: Split one table into yearly or monthly partitions
sql-memo.ddl-partition-note: The partition key must be part of every unique index, partitioned tables cannot have foreign keys, and pruning needs the key in the predicate
sql-memo.c-pk-desc: Unique and not null; in InnoDB it is the clustered index
sql-memo.c-pk-note: One per table; keep it short and increasing to avoid page splits, and never store an update-prone value in it
sql-memo.c-fk-desc: Referential integrity with separate delete and update rules
sql-memo.c-unique-desc: Business uniqueness, and an index at the same time
sql-memo.c-unique-note: Multiple NULLs are allowed because NULLs never compare equal, so unique-plus-nullable cannot express at most one live row; use a generated column or a partial index
sql-memo.c-notnull-desc: Forbid NULL, pair with a default
sql-memo.c-notnull-note: NULL complicates counting, comparison and index statistics; prefer 0 or '' where they carry the meaning
sql-memo.c-default-desc: Value used when the column is omitted
sql-memo.c-default-note: Expression defaults need parentheses and 8.0.13+; BLOB, TEXT and JSON cannot take a literal default
sql-memo.c-check-note: Parsed but ignored before 8.0.16; adding one to a legacy table fails on existing dirty rows
sql-memo.c-show-desc: Read primary, foreign and check constraints from the information schema
sql-memo.idx-create-desc: Three entry points, two deletion forms
sql-memo.idx-create-note: Index names are unique per table; keep adds and drops in separate clauses of the same ALTER to avoid mistakes
sql-memo.idx-composite-desc: The B-tree is ordered by column sequence, so skipping the left column loses the index
sql-memo.idx-composite-note: Columns after a range predicate cannot narrow the scan; put equality columns first, the range column last, sort columns next
sql-memo.idx-prefix-desc: Index only the first N characters
sql-memo.idx-prefix-note: Shorter prefixes save space but lose selectivity and can never be covering; TEXT and BLOB require a length
sql-memo.idx-covering-desc: All requested columns live in the index, so no row lookback
sql-memo.idx-covering-note: Only Extra: Using index proves it; SELECT * destroys the benefit
sql-memo.idx-fulltext-desc: Tokenized search with natural-language and boolean modes
sql-memo.idx-fulltext-note: CJK text needs the ngram parser (minimum token 2); stopwords and ft_min_word_len change what you can find
sql-memo.idx-fulltext-diff: PostgreSQL uses tsvector with a GIN index or pg_trgm, SQL Server has separate FULLTEXT CATALOGs, Oracle uses CONTAINS
sql-memo.idx-spatial-note: The column must be NOT NULL with an SRID; distance functions without index support scan everything
sql-memo.idx-function-desc: Index an expression, backed by a hidden virtual column
sql-memo.idx-function-note: Since 8.0.13 and requires an extra pair of parentheses; the query expression must match the definition exactly
sql-memo.idx-function-diff: PostgreSQL writes CREATE INDEX ON t (lower(email)), SQL Server needs a persisted computed column, Oracle indexes the function directly
sql-memo.idx-partial-desc: Index only rows meeting a condition
sql-memo.idx-partial-diff: MySQL has no indexed WHERE clause and needs a generated column; PostgreSQL supports it natively and SQL Server calls it a filtered index
sql-memo.idx-invisible-desc: Still maintained, hidden from the optimizer — the safe way to test a drop
sql-memo.idx-invisible-note: Primary keys and indexes backing unique constraints cannot be made invisible; observe for a while before really dropping
sql-memo.idx-show-desc: List indexes, column order and cardinality
sql-memo.idx-useless-title: Twelve ways to lose an index
sql-memo.idx-useless-desc: Checklist for writing and reviewing SQL
sql-memo.v-create-desc: Name a query for reuse; OR REPLACE updates the definition
sql-memo.v-select-title: Query a view like a table
sql-memo.v-select-desc: Views store no data; they expand at query time
sql-memo.v-select-note: With MERGE semantics the outer predicates push down and indexes still apply; aggregates, UNION or DISTINCT force the temp-table path and cost far more
sql-memo.v-algorithm-desc: MERGE expands inline, TEMPTABLE materializes; SQL SECURITY picks whose rights apply
sql-memo.v-update-desc: Simple views accept INSERT and UPDATE
sql-memo.v-update-note: Views with aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, UNION, window functions, constants or a repeated base column are not updatable; WITH CHECK OPTION blocks writes that would vanish
sql-memo.v-materialized-desc: Summary table refreshed by an event or trigger
sql-memo.v-materialized-diff: PostgreSQL has MATERIALIZED VIEW with REFRESH CONCURRENTLY, Oracle has materialized views, SQL Server approximates them with indexed views
sql-memo.txn-basic-desc: Bundle statements into one atomic unit
sql-memo.txn-basic-note: Clients default to autocommit=1; a BEGIN without COMMIT rolls everything back, which connection pools hide well
sql-memo.txn-savepoint-desc: Roll back only part of a transaction
sql-memo.txn-autocommit-desc: Disable autocommit, set isolation and pin a snapshot
sql-memo.txn-autocommit-note: START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT lets several connections read the same instant — useful for coordinated dumps
sql-memo.txn-isolation-desc: Each level rules out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads or phantoms
sql-memo.txn-isolation-note: InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ and prevents most phantoms with gap locks plus MVCC; PostgreSQL and SQL Server default to READ COMMITTED
sql-memo.txn-for-update-desc: Take an exclusive or shared lock, optionally NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED
sql-memo.txn-for-update-note: Only meaningful inside a transaction and locks the index records it touches; an unindexed predicate escalates to scanning and locking far more rows
sql-memo.txn-optimistic-desc: Conditional update on a version or status column
sql-memo.txn-mvcc-desc: Plain SELECTs take no lock and read an undo snapshot
sql-memo.txn-mvcc-note: Current reads (FOR UPDATE, UPDATE, DELETE) see the latest row and lock it, snapshot reads see history; mixing them produces apparent inconsistencies
sql-memo.txn-deadlock-desc: Read the latest deadlock report and current waits
sql-memo.txn-deadlock-note: Access tables and rows in the same order everywhere, keep transactions short and make predicates hit indexes — the three classic fixes
sql-memo.txn-long-desc: Find the oldest transaction and its connection
sql-memo.txn-implicit-desc: Each of these ends the current transaction
sql-memo.txn-implicit-note: A DDL in the middle of a transaction means the first half is already durable and cannot be rolled back
sql-memo.dcl-user-desc: A user is the pair of name plus allowed host
sql-memo.dcl-user-note: 'app'@'%' and 'app'@'localhost' are separate accounts with separate passwords and grants; check which row a connection matched
sql-memo.dcl-grant-desc: Grant at database, table or column granularity
sql-memo.dcl-grant-note: Since 8.0 GRANT no longer creates users implicitly; production accounts should never get DROP, FILE, SUPER or GRANT OPTION
sql-memo.dcl-role-note: Roles are not activated automatically; set DEFAULT ROLE or grant with ADMIN OPTION
sql-memo.dcl-flush-desc: Reload the grant cache after editing mysql.* by hand
sql-memo.dcl-flush-note: Not needed for GRANT or CREATE USER; only required after direct DML on the privilege tables
sql-memo.dcl-limit-desc: Connection caps, expiry and failed-login lockout
sql-memo.dcl-pwd-policy-note: In 8.0 you must INSTALL COMPONENT first; changing the variables alone does nothing
sql-memo.r-delimiter-desc: Needed because routine bodies contain semicolons
sql-memo.r-delimiter-note: DELIMITER is a mysql CLI command, not SQL; drop it when executing through drivers or GUI tools
sql-memo.r-procedure-note: Procedures can return result sets and commit, but have no return value; call them with CALL
sql-memo.r-function-desc: A function with RETURNS and characteristics
sql-memo.r-function-note: Must RETURN a scalar and cannot return a result set; with binlog enabled, omitting DETERMINISTIC / READS SQL DATA makes creation fail
sql-memo.r-trigger-desc: Row-level BEFORE / AFTER hooks with OLD and NEW
sql-memo.r-trigger-note: Before 8.0.32 only one trigger per timing and event per table; cascade actions do not fire triggers, and business logic hidden here is hard to debug
sql-memo.r-cursor-desc: Process a result set row by row
sql-memo.r-cursor-note: Declaration order is variables, then cursors, then handlers — reversing it is a syntax error; row-by-row processing is far slower than set-based SQL
sql-memo.r-event-note: Requires event_scheduler=ON, which is not persisted across restarts unless set in config; complex schedules belong in an external job system
sql-memo.r-show-desc: List procedures and functions with their definitions
sql-memo.m-show-desc: The SHOW family and switching databases
sql-memo.m-structure-desc: Columns, DDL, indexes and table status
sql-memo.m-cols-desc: Type, nullability, default and comment from the information schema
sql-memo.m-size-desc: Rank tables by data plus index footprint
sql-memo.m-size-note: TABLE_ROWS is an InnoDB estimate that can be off by double digits; use COUNT(*) when the number matters
sql-memo.m-session-desc: Current database, user, activity and killing connections
sql-memo.m-session-note: KILL rolls back the transaction, and rolling back a huge one can take longer than letting it finish
sql-memo.m-engines-desc: Available storage engines, charsets and collations
sql-memo.m-search-schema-desc: Search the information schema for a column name
sql-memo.m-fk-check-desc: List which tables reference this one
sql-memo.p-explain-desc: Default, JSON, TREE and real execution
sql-memo.p-explain-note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the statement, so on a DML it performs the change — wrap it in a transaction and roll back
sql-memo.p-type-desc: Access methods ordered from best to worst
sql-memo.p-cols-desc: Focus on key, key_len, rows, filtered and Extra
sql-memo.p-page-note: OFFSET scans and discards, so later pages get slower; infinite feeds should key off the last seen value
sql-memo.p-batch-desc: Multi-row INSERT and LOAD DATA are the fast paths
sql-memo.p-batch-note: JDBC additionally needs rewriteBatchedStatements=true or executeBatch still sends one statement at a time
sql-memo.p-slowlog-desc: Enable it and set the threshold
sql-memo.p-analyze-desc: Refresh optimizer stats and reclaim space
sql-memo.p-hint-desc: Pin join order and force indexes
sql-memo.p-hint-note: FORCE INDEX hard-codes a plan that can become worse as data shifts; always compare with EXPLAIN first. The query cache is gone in 8.0, so SQL_NO_CACHE is meaningless
sql-memo.p-rules-desc: Checklist for development and routine review
sql-memo.b-dump-desc: By database, table, schema only or data only
sql-memo.b-dump-note: A password on the command line is visible in the process list; type it interactively or use --defaults-extra-file
sql-memo.b-consistent-note: --single-transaction only works for InnoDB and conflicts with --lock-tables; --master-data was replaced by --source-data
sql-memo.b-import-desc: Redirection, -e source, or a decompressing pipe
sql-memo.b-export-csv-note: The path must sit inside secure_file_priv and the file must not exist; for local export prefer the client's --tab
sql-memo.b-binlog-desc: List, slice by time and replay
sql-memo.b-binlog-note: Point-in-time recovery means full backup then forward replay; use ROW format so the log is order-safe
sql-memo.b-login-client-desc: External password file, forced TLS and key retrieval
sql-memo.d-paging-note: SQL Server's OFFSET FETCH mandates ORDER BY; Oracle's ROWNUM is assigned before sorting, so a naive WHERE fetches the wrong page
sql-memo.d-autoincrement-note: None of IDENTITY / AUTO_INCREMENT guarantees gapless values; rollbacks and restarts leave holes, so use a separate sequence table when numbers must be contiguous
sql-memo.d-upsert-note: MySQL fires on any primary or unique key clash, so with several unique keys the matched row is unpredictable; MERGE needs extra locking hints under concurrency
sql-memo.d-concat-note: The portable recipe is CONCAT plus explicit IFNULL/COALESCE; do not rely on || or + semantics
sql-memo.d-quote-note: MySQL treats double quotes as strings unless ANSI_QUOTES is on; keep string literals single-quoted everywhere
sql-memo.d-dateformat-desc: The biggest source of cross-database rewrites
sql-memo.d-dateformat-note: SQL Server's DATEDIFF counts boundary crossings rather than elapsed time, so year differences are often off by one
sql-memo.d-null-func-desc: IFNULL / NVL / ISNULL versus portable COALESCE
sql-memo.d-cast-desc: CAST is portable, CONVERT is not
sql-memo.d-cast-note: MySQL silently turns a non-numeric string into 0 while PostgreSQL and SQL Server raise an error — a frequent migration failure
sql-memo.d-json-desc: Extraction and expansion in four dialects
sql-memo.d-json-note: PostgreSQL's json type stores only — the operators and GIN indexes need jsonb; SQL Server had no JSON column type through 2022
sql-memo.d-alter-desc: Multiple actions, renames and type changes
sql-memo.d-alter-note: Split migration scripts per dialect; PostgreSQL in particular requires a USING expression when the cast is not implicit
sql-memo.d-support-desc: Which version introduced window functions, CTEs, JSON and partial indexes
sql-memo.pg-psql-desc: Backslash commands are client features, not SQL
sql-memo.pg-admin-desc: How ROLE relates to USER and database-level grants
sql-memo.pg-admin-note: USER is just ROLE WITH LOGIN; privileges do not retroactively apply to existing objects, so use ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES
sql-memo.pg-types-desc: Identity, arrays, JSONB and network types
sql-memo.pg-syntax-desc: ILIKE, DISTINCT ON, generate_series, UPDATE FROM
sql-memo.pg-syntax-note: DISTINCT ON requires a matching leading ORDER BY expression
sql-memo.pg-index-note: CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, and a failed build leaves an INVALID index you must drop and rebuild
sql-memo.pg-conf-desc: Key settings in postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf
sql-memo.pg-conf-note: listen_addresses, max_connections and shared_buffers need a restart; reload alone will not apply them
sql-memo.pg-docker-note: Environment variables and init scripts only run when the data directory is empty; delete the volume to reconfigure
sql-memo.pg-maintain-desc: VACUUM, ANALYZE, REINDEX and size queries
sql-memo.pg-pitfalls-desc: Identifier folding, aborted transactions, remote access and Docker
sql-memo.sec-injection-desc: The root cause is always parsing data as code
sql-memo.sec-injection-note: Escaping helpers are only a fallback and depend on the connection charset; only prepared statements keep values out of the parser
sql-memo.sec-framework-desc: MyBatis #{} versus ${} is night and day
sql-memo.sec-framework-note: Dynamic table names, column names and sort directions cannot be parameterized; map them through a whitelist
sql-memo.sec-minimal-desc: Scope application accounts to one database and a few actions
sql-memo.pr-table-desc: Naming, primary keys, nullability and type choices
sql-memo.pr-index-desc: Column order, count limits and verification
sql-memo.pr-sql-desc: Hard conventions for queries, writes and changes
sql-memo.pr-change-note: Online DDL still takes a metadata lock, so an open long transaction will queue the DDL and block everything behind it; check INNODB_TRX first
sql-memo.pr-design-desc: Delete strategy, audit columns and growth path

my-download.title: Download the ZIP (noinstall) package
my-download.detail: Pick the zip archive at the bottom of the Downloads section rather than the online installer; the x64 ZIP is portable, which makes version swaps and whole-directory backups trivial
my-download.code-note: The version number moves with each release; 8.4 is the current LTS line and the file name always ends in -winx64.zip

my-extract.title: Extract to a fixed location
my-extract.detail: Keep the path free of spaces and non-ASCII characters; separating the program directory from the data directory means you can reinstall without touching data

my-path.title: Add bin to PATH
my-path.detail: Run setx from an elevated prompt, or append it through System Properties to Environment Variables; open a new window afterwards
my-path.note: Only needed for machines where you type mysqld commands; a service does not depend on PATH

my-ini.title: Write my.ini
my-ini.detail: The Windows service reads it from the basedir root; use forward slashes in paths or double every backslash
my-ini.note: lower_case_table_names must be decided before initialization — changing it later prevents the server from starting — and datadir must be empty

my-init.title: Initialize the data directory
my-init.detail: This creates the system tablespaces and the mysql schema; running it twice fails, so clear datadir before retrying
my-init.code-insecure: Preferred on dev boxes: root starts with no password and you set one immediately
my-init.code-secure: Secure mode: a random temporary password is written to the error log and expires on first login
my-init.find: Only needed after --initialize: grab the temporary password from the log

my-service.title: Install as a Windows service and start it
my-service.detail: Use an elevated prompt, and note that --install must come before --defaults-file or the service ignores your configuration
my-service.note: If the service will not start, read the tail of mysqld.err — it is almost always a path or datadir permission problem

my-login.title: First login and root password
my-login.detail: After --initialize-insecure just press enter at the password prompt; set a real password immediately and never expose an empty one

my-verify.title: Verify charset and key settings
my-verify.detail: The three checks confirm the charset chain, that CJK text is stored as multiple bytes, and the isolation and autocommit defaults

my-docker.title: Run it with Docker
my-docker.detail: The official image keeps data in /var/lib/mysql and reads extra options from /etc/mysql/conf.d/*.cnf; server options can also be appended to the container command

my-trouble.title: Four common failures
my-trouble.detail: Match the symptom to the fix instead of reinstalling
my-trouble.denied: Access denied: 'root'@'localhost' and 'root'@'127.0.0.1' are different accounts, so pin one transport first
my-trouble.pubkey: Public Key Retrieval is not allowed: the 8.0 default auth plugin needs the RSA public key; add this flag or use --get-server-public-key
my-trouble.plugin: Old Navicat or drivers complaining about the auth plugin: fall the account back to mysql_native_password (already deprecated)
my-trouble.forget: Lost root password: stop the service, run the ALTER USER statement through --init-file, then delete the file and start normally

pg-download.title: Get the installer
pg-download.detail: The official Windows page forwards to EDB: the interactive installer bundles pgAdmin 4 and Stack Builder, while the plain binaries ZIP contains just the server
pg-download.note: Check the version right after installing to confirm you got a supported major release

pg-installer.title: Installer wizard choices
pg-installer.detail: Put installation and data directories on a path without spaces or CJK characters; the superuser defaults to postgres and its password is mandatory
pg-installer.service: The service name embeds the major version and architecture — confirm it locally instead of trusting documentation

pg-path.title: Add bin to PATH
pg-path.detail: Only needed if you run psql, pg_dump or initdb from the command line; GUI connections do not care

pg-initdb.title: Initialize and control the server from the CLI
pg-initdb.detail: Without the installer: initdb the data directory, then start and stop with pg_ctl; the server process must not run under a built-in administrator account
pg-initdb.note: With --locale=C you must pass --encoding=UTF8 explicitly, otherwise initdb falls back to SQL_ASCII and CJK text is corrupted on write
pg-initdb.start: -l points at the log file; read it whenever startup fails

pg-psql.title: Connect and self test
pg-psql.detail: psql is the default local administration entry point; meta-commands start with a backslash
pg-psql.note: The \d family is a psql client feature, not SQL, so it does not exist in other tools

pg-conf.title: Edit the two configuration files
pg-conf.detail: Both live in the data directory; remote access requires changing postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf together — one alone will not work

pg-hba.note: By default local connections use ident/peer and there is no remote entry; switch to scram-sha-256 for password logins and never combine 0.0.0.0/0 with md5

pg-reload.title: Apply configuration
pg-reload.detail: Reload only re-reads files; parameters marked as restart-required stay pending
pg-reload.note: This query lists every parameter that changed on disk but has not been applied yet

pg-remote.title: Open remote access
pg-remote.detail: The three steps are ordered: listen_addresses to *, add a host entry in pg_hba.conf, then allow port 5432 in the firewall
pg-remote.note: On Windows, pg_hba.conf changes take effect for new connections immediately — no reload needed, unlike Linux

pg-docker.title: PostgreSQL in Docker
pg-docker.detail: For image versions 17 and below, mount the volume at /var/lib/postgresql/data and point PGDATA at a nested directory
pg-docker.note17: Without the nested PGDATA the mount hides the image's directory layout and data stops persisting
pg-docker.note18: Since 18 the image declares the volume at /var/lib/postgresql, so mount that directly and drop the nested path

pg-trouble.title: Three common failures
pg-trouble.detail: Authentication, encoding and configuration that seems ignored
pg-trouble.auth: password authentication failed: either the password is wrong or it was stored as an md5 hash while pg_hba demands scram — just reset it
pg-trouble.enc: Garbled CJK text: check the database and client encoding, then SET client_encoding if needed
pg-trouble.volume: Environment variable changes ignored: the image only initializes an empty data directory, so remove the volume

sql-memo.str-concat-desc: Join strings; the _WS variant adds a separator and skips NULLs
sql-memo.str-concat-note: CONCAT returns NULL if any argument is NULL, so wrap values in IFNULL or reach for CONCAT_WS
sql-memo.str-concat-diff: PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server use || (Oracle treats NULL as empty, PostgreSQL propagates it); SQL Server 2012+ CONCAT ignores NULLs
sql-memo.b-restore-table-note: Rename the damaged table away first so it stops taking writes, then reload; compare charset and sql_mode before restoring across major versions
sql-memo.b-user-grants-note: This dumps only the privilege tables, without definers or routines; restoring a 5.7 account table into 8.0 yields logins that fail on the auth plugin field
sql-memo.c-fk-note: Foreign key columns get an automatic index; high-concurrency and sharded systems often drop foreign keys and enforce integrity in the application instead
sql-memo.cs-where-note: An inline COLLATE affects only this comparison and leaves the column definition alone; make the column _bin if you always need exact matching
sql-memo.v-algorithm-note: TEMPTABLE views cannot be updated and block predicate pushdown; if the DEFINER account is dropped, every query through the view starts failing
sql-memo.v-drop-note: Dropping a view leaves base tables and data untouched; CREATE OR REPLACE swaps the definition silently, so watch out for views you did not own
sql-memo.ddl-add-col-diff: PostgreSQL supports ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS and merges several actions with commas; SQL Server allows one action per ALTER; Oracle lists multiple columns inside MODIFY
sql-memo.ddl-modify-change-diff: PostgreSQL and SQL Server rename with ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE / RENAME COLUMN and need USING when the cast is not implicit; SQL Server's sp_rename is discouraged
